title: Unit Testing
description: Write fast, reliable tests that catch real bugs — principles first, then JUnit 5, Mockito, pytest and unittest.mock in practice.
keyIdeas: A unit test is **fast, isolated, repeatable and self-checking** — its job is to catch regressions in seconds.
Every test is **Arrange → Act → Assert**, checks one behavior, and has a name that explains its failure.
Test the happy path, the **boundaries** and the error cases — through the public API, not the internals.
Assert exact values: `assertEquals(expected, actual)` in JUnit, plain `assert` in pytest.
Use test doubles for slow or unpredictable boundaries, inject them through the constructor, and **don't over-mock**.
Coverage finds untested code but isn't a goal; flaky tests come from uncontrolled time, randomness and shared state.

concepts.label: Unit test
concepts.summary: A small automated check of one function or class that is fast, isolated from real I/O and repeatable, giving regression safety.

concepts.label: Self-checking test
concepts.summary: The test decides pass or fail itself with an assertion; printing a result for a human to read checks nothing.

concepts.label: Arrange-Act-Assert
concepts.summary: Set up the inputs, perform the one action under test, then check the outcome, in that order.

concepts.label: One behavior per test
concepts.summary: Each test checks one behavior and is named for the situation and expected result, so a failure says exactly what broke.

concepts.label: Edge cases
concepts.summary: Besides the happy path, test boundaries (at and just past each limit), empty or null inputs and error cases, where bugs cluster.

concepts.label: Behavior, not implementation
concepts.summary: Test through the public API and check observable results, not private helpers or how the result was computed, so refactors do not break tests.

concepts.label: Exact assertion
concepts.summary: Assert the exact, independently known expected value with the most specific assertion (approx for floats), not just "not None".

concepts.label: Expected vs actual
concepts.summary: A failure report shows what the test expected and what the code produced, which depends on passing expected and actual in the right order.

concepts.label: Test discovery
concepts.summary: The runner finds tests by annotation (JUnit 5's org.junit.jupiter.api.Test) or by name (pytest's test_* functions); anything else silently never runs.

concepts.label: Fresh state per test
concepts.summary: Each test gets its own new objects (@BeforeEach, a new test-class instance, function-scoped fixtures), so tests cannot affect each other.

concepts.label: Asserting exceptions
concepts.summary: assertThrows, pytest.raises and assertFailsWith pass only if the code throws the expected exception, and code after the throw never runs.

concepts.label: Parameterized test
concepts.summary: One test method runs once per row of inputs and expected results, each reported as its own test.

concepts.label: pytest fixture
concepts.summary: Setup code that pytest injects by parameter name, rebuilt for every test by default (scope widens how long it is shared).

concepts.label: Kotlin test idioms
concepts.summary: Kotlin tests run on JUnit 5 with backtick names, assertFailsWith<T> and @JvmStatic companion functions for @BeforeAll.

concepts.label: Test double
concepts.summary: A stand-in you control for a real dependency (database, network, clock, email): a stub, mock, fake or spy.

concepts.label: Stub
concepts.summary: A double that returns canned answers to feed data into the code under test.

concepts.label: Mock
concepts.summary: A double that records calls so the test can verify what the code sent out, for commands with no useful return value.

concepts.label: Dependency injection
concepts.summary: Passing dependencies in, usually through the constructor, instead of building them inside lets a test hand in a double.

concepts.label: Patching
concepts.summary: unittest.mock.patch temporarily swaps a name, and must target it where it is used (billing.charge_card), not where it is defined.

concepts.label: Over-mocking
concepts.summary: Mock only boundaries like network and databases; mocking simple values or verifying stubbed calls tests how, not what.

concepts.label: Red-green-refactor
concepts.summary: Test-driven development: write a failing test, make it pass with the simplest code, then refactor while staying green; for bugs, reproduce first.

concepts.label: Flaky test
concepts.summary: A test that passes or fails with no code change because it depends on time, randomness, order, shared state or real I/O.

concepts.label: Code coverage
concepts.summary: The share of lines or branches your tests ran: good for finding untested code, a poor target because running is not checking.

concepts.label: Test pyramid
concepts.summary: Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests against real databases or HTTP, and a few end-to-end tests at the top.

units.title: Testing foundations
units.description: What makes a test worth having, how to structure it, and which cases to pick.

lessons.title: What a unit test is (and why bother)
lessons.takeaway: A unit test is a tiny program that checks one behavior in milliseconds — fast, isolated, repeatable and self-checking — so you can change code without fear.

steps.title: Code that checks code
steps.body:
A **unit test** is a small piece of code that runs a small piece of your code — a *unit*, usually one function or class — and checks the result automatically.

```python
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

def test_add():
    assert add(2, 3) == 5
```

A test runner (pytest, JUnit) runs every test and reports **pass** or **fail**. No reading printouts, no clicking through the app.

steps.title: Four properties of a good unit test
steps.body:
- **Fast** — milliseconds each, so you can run thousands on every change
- **Isolated** — no real network, database or shared files; one test can't break another
- **Repeatable** — same result every run, on every machine
- **Self-checking** — the test decides pass/fail itself; no human inspects output

The payoff is **regression safety**: when you refactor or add a feature, the suite tells you within seconds if you broke something that used to work.

steps.prompt: Which of these is **not** a self-checking test?
choices: `print(total([1, 2]))` — then a developer eyeballs the output
steps.explanation: A self-checking test encodes the expected result, so the runner can decide pass/fail on its own. Printing makes a *human* the assertion — they get bored, skim, and miss the one wrong number.

steps.prompt: `discount` is broken: VIPs get 2% off instead of 20%. The test below should catch that, but the suite reports `1 passed`. Click the line in the **test** that lets the bug slip through.
fixes: Change line 7 to `assert discount(100, "VIP") is not None`
steps.hint: What does the test runner do with printed output?
steps.explanation: The test only **prints** the result, so it can never fail: it isn't self-checking. With `assert discount(100, "VIP") == 80` the runner compares for you and reports `assert 98.0 == 80`. `assert discount(...)` and `is not None` pass for 98.0 (any non-zero number counts as true), and printing `False` still leaves the decision to a human who isn't looking.

steps.prompt: A test calls a real payment API over the internet, takes 4 seconds, and sometimes fails when the Wi-Fi drops. Which unit-test properties does it break?
choices: None — it asserts on the result, so it's a fine unit test
steps.explanation: It's slow (seconds, not milliseconds), depends on an outside system (not isolated), and its result depends on the network (not repeatable). It may be a useful *integration* test, but a unit test would replace the payment API with a stand-in.

steps.title: Regression safety in action
steps.problem: You have the test `assert discount(100, "VIP") == 80`. Months later a teammate "simplifies" `discount` and accidentally gives VIPs 2% off instead of 20%. What happens?
steps: The teammate runs the suite — or CI runs it automatically on push.
`discount(100, "VIP")` now returns 98, so the assertion `98 == 80` fails.
The report names the failing test and shows both values, pointing straight at the broken behavior.
steps.answer: The bug is caught **in seconds, before it ships**. Tests remember how the code is supposed to behave, so nobody has to.

steps.prompt: Why does speed matter so much for unit tests?
choices: Test runners refuse to run tests slower than one second
Fast tests get run constantly — on every save or commit — so bugs are caught minutes after they're written
steps.explanation: A suite that runs in seconds gets run all the time; one that takes 20 minutes gets run "later" (or never). The sooner a bug is caught, the cheaper it is to fix — you still remember what you just changed.

lessons.title: Arrange, Act, Assert — and good names
lessons.takeaway: Shape every test as Arrange → Act → Assert, check one behavior per test, and name it so the failure explains itself.

steps.title: Three parts
steps.body:
Almost every good test has the same shape:

- **Arrange** — set up the inputs and objects
- **Act** — call the one thing you're testing (usually a single line)
- **Assert** — check the outcome

```java
@Test
void withdrawReducesBalance() {
    Account account = new Account(100);   // Arrange

    account.withdraw(30);                 // Act

    assertEquals(70, account.getBalance()); // Assert
}
```

Blank lines between the parts are enough; the comments are optional.

steps.prompt:
Which line is the **Act** step?

```python
def test_cart_total_includes_tax():
    cart = Cart(tax_rate=0.10)          # line 1
    cart.add(Item("book", price=20))    # line 2
    total = cart.total()                # line 3
    assert total == pytest.approx(22)   # line 4
```
steps.explanation: Lines 1–2 build the situation (Arrange). Line 3 calls the behavior the test is about, `total()` (Act). Line 4 checks it (Assert). Adding the item is *setup* here, because the test is about the total, not about adding.
steps.hint: What behavior does the test name say it checks?

steps.prompt: pytest runs this test. Step through its three parts and predict the values when asked.
steps.code:
def cart_total(cart, coupon):
    return sum(cart) - coupon

def test_coupon_is_subtracted():
    cart = []
    cart.append(20)
    cart.append(15)
    coupon = 5

    total = cart_total(cart, coupon)

    assert total == 30

frames.note: **Act:** one call to the code under test.

steps.explanation: Lines 5–8 **arrange** the inputs, line 10 is the single **act** (the call under test), and line 12 **asserts** the outcome: 20 + 15 − 5 = 30. A passing `assert` does nothing at all; a failing one stops the test with an `AssertionError`.
steps.hint: The cart holds 20 and 15; the coupon takes 5 off the sum.

steps.prompt: `Cart.total()` works correctly, yet this test fails. It should pass: a book priced 20 plus 10% tax totals 22. Click the line with the bug.
steps.code:
def test_cart_total_includes_tax():
    cart = Cart(tax_rate=0.10)
    total = cart.total()
    cart.add(Item("book", price=20))
    assert total == pytest.approx(22)
steps.hint: Label each line Arrange, Act or Assert. Are they in that order?
steps.explanation: The Act (`cart.total()`) runs before the Arrange is finished, so it totals an **empty** cart and stores 0.0. Adding the book afterwards doesn't change the number already in `total`. Moving the Act below the `add` gives Arrange → Act → Assert and a total of 22. Changing the tax rate or the price still totals an empty cart, and calling `cart.total()` again without storing it leaves `total` at 0.0.

steps.title: One behavior per test
steps.body:
A test should check **one behavior**. A test that goes act-assert-act-assert-act-assert has two problems:

- The first failing assertion stops the test, so everything after it goes **unchecked**.
- Its name can't describe it all, so a failure tells you little.

Several asserts are fine when they describe *one* outcome (say, both coordinates of a returned point). Several *acts* usually mean you want several tests.

steps.title: Splitting a test that does too much
steps.problem:
```python
def test_stack():
    s = Stack()
    s.push(1)
    assert s.peek() == 1
    s.pop()
    assert s.is_empty()
    with pytest.raises(IndexError):
        s.pop()
```
steps: Spot the separate behaviors: peek shows the last push, popping the last item empties the stack, and popping an empty stack raises.
Give each its own test with its own Arrange: `test_peek_returns_last_pushed_item`, `test_pop_last_item_leaves_stack_empty`, `test_pop_on_empty_stack_raises_index_error`.
Now if pop-on-empty breaks, exactly one test fails, and its name says what's wrong.
steps.answer: Three small tests, one Act each. A failure points at **one behavior** instead of "something somewhere in test_stack".

steps.prompt: A long test fails on its **first** assertion. It has four more act-assert pairs after that. What do you learn about those later behaviors?
choices: Nothing — the test stopped at the first failed assertion
The runner retries each of them separately
steps.explanation: A failed assertion throws (`AssertionError` / `AssertionFailedError`), ending the test right there. The later checks never ran — they might be broken too, and you won't know until you fix the first one. Separate tests report independently.

steps.title: Names that explain failures
steps.body:
When a test fails, its name is the first thing you read. Good names say **the situation** and **the expected result**:

- `test_withdraw_more_than_balance_raises_error`
- `emptyCartHasZeroTotal()`
- Bad: `test1`, `testWithdraw`, `testCartWorks`

A handy template: *action_situation_expectedResult*. Long names are fine — you never type them anywhere else.

steps.prompt: Which test name is most useful when it fails?
steps.explanation: It tells you the input situation (month 13) and the expected behavior (raises ValueError) without opening the file. "Works correctly" says nothing — every test claims that.

lessons.title: What to test: the 80/20 of test cases
lessons.takeaway: For each behavior, test the happy path, the boundaries and the error cases — through the public API, never the private internals.

steps.title: Three kinds of cases
steps.body:
You can't test every input. These cases catch most bugs:

- **Happy path** — a normal, typical input works
- **Boundaries & edge cases** — exactly at a limit and just either side of it; empty, zero, one, negative, `null`/`None`, huge
- **Error cases** — invalid input is rejected the way it should be (an exception, an error result)

Bugs cluster at boundaries: writing `>` where you meant `>=` is one of the most common bugs there is.

steps.title: Picking cases for a rule
steps.problem: `is_adult(age)` should return `True` for ages 18 and up, and raise `ValueError` for negative ages. Which inputs should you test?
steps: Happy path: a clearly typical value on each side — 30 → `True`, 10 → `False`.
Boundary: the exact edge and its neighbor — 18 → `True`, 17 → `False`. Also 0, the smallest valid age.
Error case: -1 → raises `ValueError`.
steps.answer: About six tests (10, 17, 18, 30, 0, -1) catch nearly every realistic bug in this function — including `>` written instead of `>=`.

steps.prompt: The implementation is `return age > 18` (the bug: it should be `>=`). Which test catches it?
steps.explanation: Only at exactly 18 do `>` and `>=` disagree. 30, 5 and 17 give the same answer under both, so those tests pass with the bug still in. This is why boundary tests earn their keep.

steps.prompt: Tests for `average(numbers)`: `average([2, 4]) == 3` and `average([5]) == 5`. Which important edge case is missing?
steps.explanation: Dividing by `len([])` is division by zero — the classic crash. Decide what *should* happen (raise a clear error? return 0?) and pin it down with a test. The other choices are just more happy paths.
steps.hint: Think "empty, zero, one, many".

steps.prompt: Passwords must be 8 to 64 characters long (inclusive). You already test lengths 7, 8 and 64. Which length should you test next to cover the other boundary's **invalid** side?
steps.explanation: Each boundary deserves a test on both sides: 7 (invalid) / 8 (valid) at the bottom, 64 (valid) / **65** (invalid) at the top. A `<= 64` written as `< 65` is fine; one written as `<= 65` is caught only by 65.

steps.prompt: Passwords must be 8 to 64 characters long (inclusive). All three tests pass, but users with a 64-character password are rejected. Click the line with the bug.
steps.hint: Which boundary do the tests never touch?
steps.explanation: `< 64` excludes 64 itself, the classic off-by-one. The tests only probe the **lower** boundary (7 and 8) and a typical value, so the upper one goes unchecked. `<= 64` accepts 8 to 64 exactly. `8 < len(pw)` now rejects 8, `7 <= ...` accepts 7, and `<= 65` accepts 65. Pin it down by adding tests for 64 (valid) and 65 (invalid).

steps.title: Test behavior, not implementation
steps.body:
Test through the **public API** — the methods real callers use — and check **observable results**: return values, state you can read back, exceptions thrown, messages sent to collaborators.

Don't call private helpers directly, and don't assert *how* the result was computed (which internal list was used, how many times a helper ran). Such tests break on every refactor even though nothing is wrong, and they make people afraid to improve the code.

steps.prompt: Which test is most likely to break during a harmless refactor of a sorting function?
choices: Checks that sorting an empty list returns an empty list
Calls the private helper `_partition()` directly and checks which pivot index it picks
steps.explanation: Switch the algorithm from quicksort to merge sort and `_partition` disappears — that test breaks although sorting still works perfectly. The other three test *what* sort promises, so they survive any correct rewrite.

lessons.title: Good assertions & reading failures
lessons.takeaway: Assert the exact expected value with the most specific assertion available, and read every failure as "expected X, but was Y" before touching code.

steps.title: Assert precisely
steps.body:
A test is only as good as its assertions. Weak ones let bugs through:

- `assert result is not None` — passes for almost any wrong answer
- `assertTrue(items.size() > 0)` — passes with the wrong items

Prefer the **exact expected value**: `assert result == [1, 2, 3]`, `assertEquals("Ada", user.getName())`.

Also use the most specific assertion you have: `assertEquals(a, b)` beats `assertTrue(a.equals(b))` because its failure shows both values instead of just "expected true".

steps.prompt: `slugify("Hello World")` should return `"hello-world"`. A buggy version returns `"hello world"`. Which test catches the bug?
steps.explanation: `"hello world"` is a non-None string of length 11 — exactly like `"hello-world"`. All three weak assertions pass with the bug. Only comparing to the exact expected value catches it.

steps.prompt: `total_with_tax(100, 0.2)` should return 120, but it returns 100.2. The test below still passes. Click the line in the **test** that lets the bug slip through.
steps.hint: Where does the expected value come from?
steps.explanation: The expected value is computed **by the code under test**, so the test compares the function with itself and passes whatever it returns. Write the exact expected value by hand: with `expected = 120` the test fails with `assert 100.2 == 120`, as it should. `approx` still compares the function with itself, `100 + 0.2` copies the bug into the test, and `> 100` is a weak assertion that 100.2 satisfies.

steps.title: Reading a failure message
steps.body:
JUnit:

```
expected: <70> but was: <100>
```

pytest:

```
>       assert account.balance == 70
E       assert 100 == 70
E        +  where 100 = <Account object>.balance
```

Read it as a story: *the test expected 70; the code produced 100*. Before changing anything, ask: is the **code** wrong, or is the test's **expectation** wrong? Then check the test name and the Act line to see which behavior broke.

steps.title: Diagnosing a failure
steps.problem: After `account.withdraw(30)` on an account holding 100, `assertEquals(70, account.getBalance())` fails with `expected: <70> but was: <100>`. Where do you look?
steps: Expected 70, got 100: the balance didn't change **at all**.
So `withdraw` ran but had no effect. A wrong calculation would give something else, like 130 (added instead of subtracted).
Look in `withdraw` for a result that's never stored — e.g. `balance - amount;` computed but not assigned back to `balance`.
steps.answer: The actual value narrows the bug down before you even open the code: **100 means "nothing happened"**.

steps.prompt: In JUnit, someone writes `assertEquals(account.getBalance(), 70)`, and the balance is actually 100. What does the failure say?
steps.explanation: JUnit's signature is `assertEquals(expected, actual)`: it treats the *first* argument as the expected value. With the arguments swapped the test still fails, but the message claims 100 was expected — sending you hunting in the wrong direction.
steps.hint: Which argument does JUnit call "expected"?

steps.prompt: `assert 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` fails in Python. What's the right fix?
choices: Delete the test — floating-point math is unpredictable
steps.explanation: Binary floating point can't represent 0.1 exactly, so the sum is `0.30000000000000004`. Compare with a tolerance: `pytest.approx` in pytest, or `assertEquals(0.3, x, 1e-9)` (a delta) in JUnit. The `str` version still fails, and rounding to 0 would pass for almost anything.

units.title: Tools in practice
units.description: The handful of JUnit 5 and pytest features you'll use every day — plus Kotlin.

lessons.title: JUnit 5 essentials
lessons.takeaway: JUnit 5 in a nutshell: `@Test` methods, `assertEquals(expected, actual)`, `assertThrows` for errors, `@BeforeEach` for fresh setup, and `@ParameterizedTest` for tables of cases.

steps.title: A JUnit 5 test class
Exceptions and fresh setup

steps.prompt: Which line correctly tests that `parseAge("abc")` throws `NumberFormatException`?
steps.explanation: The lambda lets JUnit call `parseAge` *inside* its own try/catch. Calling `parseAge("abc")` directly as an argument throws before any assertion runs (and the swapped version doesn't even compile). The try/catch with no assertion passes even when **nothing** is thrown — the classic silent test.

steps.prompt: A `cart` is created once in a `@BeforeAll static` method and shared by the class. Test A adds an item; Test B asserts the cart is empty. What's the risk?
choices: Test B passes or fails depending on which test runs first
JUnit refuses to compile the class
None — JUnit resets static fields between tests
steps.explanation: Shared mutable state couples tests through execution order, and you shouldn't rely on JUnit's method order. Create the cart in `@BeforeEach` so every test gets its own. Keep `@BeforeAll` for expensive, *read-only* setup.

steps.title: Parameterized tests

steps.explanation: Each string in `@CsvSource` is one row, and each row is one invocation. Two strings → **2** runs (the commas *inside* a string separate the three arguments).
steps.hint: Count the strings, not the numbers.

steps.title: Turning copy-paste into a table
steps.problem: You have three near-identical tests: `isLeapYear(2024)` is true, `isLeapYear(1900)` is false, `isLeapYear(2000)` is true. Rewrite them as one parameterized test.
steps: Spot what varies: the year and the expected result. Those become the method's parameters.
Each case becomes a CSV row: `"2024, true"`, `"1900, false"`, `"2000, true"`.
The body is a single assertion. JUnit converts the text `true` to a `boolean` for you.

steps.prompt: A test method never runs — it doesn't show up as passed **or** failed. Your project uses only JUnit 5. What's the most likely cause?
choices: It's annotated with JUnit 4's `org.junit.Test` instead of `org.junit.jupiter.api.Test`
steps.explanation: The JUnit 5 engine only looks for Jupiter annotations; a JUnit 4 `@Test` is silently ignored unless the "vintage" engine is installed. A wrong auto-import is an easy way to get a test that never runs. Package-private methods are fine in JUnit 5, and `@DisplayName` is optional.
steps.hint: Check the import line.

steps.prompt: `Years.isLeapYear` follows the real calendar rules and is correct, yet this parameterized test fails. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error:
2 tests successful
1 tests failed
org.opentest4j.AssertionFailedError: expected: <false> but was: <true>
fixes: Change line 7 to `void leapYears(int year, Boolean expected) {`
steps.hint: Century years are leap years only when divisible by 400.
steps.explanation: The code is right; the **test data** is wrong. 2000 is divisible by 400, so it is a leap year: the row should read `"2000, true"`. The failure says the test expected `false` and the code returned `true`, and only two rows expect `false`. 1900 really isn't a leap year (divisible by 100 but not 400), so changing that row adds a second failure. Swapping the `assertEquals` arguments only flips the message, and `Boolean` instead of `boolean` changes nothing.

lessons.title: pytest essentials
lessons.takeaway: pytest collects `test_` functions, uses plain `assert`, injects fixtures by parameter name, and offers `parametrize` for tables and `pytest.raises` for errors.

steps.title: Plain functions, plain assert
steps.body:
```python
# test_pricing.py
import pytest
from pricing import apply_discount

def test_ten_percent_discount():
    assert apply_discount(200, 0.10) == pytest.approx(180)
```

- **Discovery:** files named `test_*.py` or `*_test.py`; functions whose names start with `test` (also methods of `Test...` classes).
- Use a plain `assert`. pytest rewrites it so a failure shows both sides of the comparison.
- Run `pytest` in the project folder; `pytest -k discount` runs only tests whose names match.

steps.prompt: In `test_cart.py`, which function will pytest collect and run as a test?
steps.explanation: Test *functions* must start with `test`. The `*_test` pattern applies to file names, not functions — so `total_test` is silently skipped as an ordinary helper.

steps.title: Fixtures

steps.prompt: Using the fixture above (default scope): Test A adds an item to `cart`. Test B, which runs after it, asserts `cart.total() == 0`. Does B pass?
choices: No — B sees A's item, because fixtures are created once per file
Yes — the fixture function runs again for each test, so B gets a new, empty cart
Only if B happens to run before A
No — two tests can't share a fixture
steps.explanation: The default fixture scope is `"function"`: one fresh value per test. Wider scopes (`scope="module"`, `"session"`) share one value — useful for expensive read-only setup, risky for anything a test modifies.

steps.prompt: Each test should get its own fresh cart, so both tests should pass. Instead the second one fails. Click the line with the bug.
steps.hint: How often does a `scope="module"` fixture run?
steps.explanation: `scope="module"` builds **one** cart for the whole file, so the second test sees the book the first test added. The default scope (`"function"`) runs the fixture again for every test. `"session"` shares the cart even more widely, `yield` only adds a place for cleanup (the cart is still shared), and `approx(0)` can't turn 22 into 0.

steps.title: Errors and tables
steps.body:
```python
def test_negative_price_rejected():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="negative"):
        apply_discount(-5, 0.10)

@pytest.mark.parametrize("price, rate, expected", [
    (200, 0.10, 180),
    (100, 0, 100),
    (50, 1, 0),
])
def test_apply_discount(price, rate, expected):
    assert apply_discount(price, rate) == pytest.approx(expected)
```

- `pytest.raises` fails the test if the block **doesn't** raise that exception; `match` checks the message with a regex.
- `parametrize` runs the test once per tuple and reports each case separately.

steps.prompt:
What's wrong with this test?

```python
def test_parse_rejects_text():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        result = parse_age("abc")
        assert result is None
```
choices: `pytest.raises` needs the function passed as a lambda
The `assert` after the raising call never runs, so it's dead code pretending to check something
steps.explanation: When `parse_age` raises, control jumps straight out of the `with` block, so the assert is skipped. Keep only the call that should raise inside `pytest.raises`; put any follow-up checks after the block (e.g. on the `ExceptionInfo` from `as exc_info`).
steps.hint: Trace what happens on the line where the exception is thrown.

steps.title: A boundary table in pytest
steps.problem: Turn the `is_adult` cases — 10, 17, 18, 30, plus -1 raising `ValueError` — into pytest tests.
steps: The valid cases share a shape (input, expected bool), so they go in one `parametrize` table.
The error case has a different shape — it raises — so it gets its own test with `pytest.raises`.
Each tuple is reported separately, e.g. `test_is_adult[18-True]`, so a failure names the exact input.

steps.prompt: Fill in the blank: `@pytest.mark.______("x, expected", [(1, 2), (2, 4)])`
steps.explanation: It's `parametrize` — note pytest's spelling, *not* "parameterize". pytest rejects the common misspellings with an error rather than silently ignoring them.

lessons.title: Testing in Kotlin
lessons.takeaway: Kotlin runs on the same JUnit 5 engine; add backtick test names and `kotlin.test` assertions like `assertFailsWith` for idiomatic tests.

steps.title: Same engine, nicer syntax
Exceptions the Kotlin way

steps.prompt: Which Kotlin assertion checks that `parse("x")` throws `NumberFormatException`?
steps.explanation: The code under test must go *inside* the lambda so `assertFailsWith` can catch what it throws. In the other options `parse("x")` runs first and its exception escapes before any assertion can handle it (and the first one doesn't compile).

steps.prompt: A Kotlin test class has the property `private val cart = ShoppingCart()`. Test A adds an item; Test B asserts the cart is empty. With JUnit 5's default lifecycle, does B pass?
choices: Yes — JUnit creates a new instance of the test class for every test method, so each test gets its own `cart`
No — class properties are shared by all tests in the class
No — a `val` property can't be modified, so `add` fails
steps.explanation: JUnit 5 defaults to one test-class instance **per method**, so property initializers re-run for each test. (Annotating the class `@TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)` changes that and makes such state shared.) `val` only fixes the *reference* — the cart object itself is still mutable.

steps.title: Data classes make assertions easy
steps.problem: `parseUser("Ada,36")` returns `User(name = "Ada", age = 36)`, where `User` is a `data class`. How should you assert the result?
steps: A `data class` generates `equals()` from its properties: two `User`s with the same name and age are equal.
So compare the whole object at once: `assertEquals(User("Ada", 36), parseUser("Ada,36"))`.
If it fails, the message prints both objects via the generated `toString()`, e.g. `User(name=Ada, age=36)` vs `User(name=Ada, age=63)`.
steps.answer: One assertion on the whole value: shorter than checking each field, and the failure shows exactly which field differs.

steps.prompt: `Prices.load()` is slow, so it should run **once** for the whole class. Instead, JUnit refuses to run the class. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error:
JUnit Jupiter ✘ TestEngine with ID 'junit-jupiter' encountered a critical issue during test discovery:
(1) [ERROR] @BeforeAll method 'public final void PriceTest.loadPrices()' must be static unless the test class is annotated with @TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS).
  ...
fixes: Wrap lines 6–9 in `companion object { ... }` and add `@JvmStatic` above line 7
steps.hint: How does Kotlin produce a Java static method?
steps.explanation: Kotlin has no `static` keyword; a `companion object` member marked `@JvmStatic` compiles to a real static method on `PriceTest`, which is what JUnit needs. Without `@JvmStatic`, the function lives only on the separate `Companion` class, so JUnit never finds it: the class runs, `load()` never happens, and the test fails with *Key apple is missing in the map*. `@JvmStatic` outside an object doesn't compile, and `private` is still not static. The alternative is `@TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)`, which lets `@BeforeAll` be a normal method.

units.title: Test doubles
units.description: Stubs, mocks and fakes: testing code that talks to the outside world.

lessons.title: Stubs, mocks, fakes and spies
lessons.takeaway: Replace slow or unpredictable dependencies with doubles — stubs feed answers in, mocks check calls going out, fakes are lightweight working versions — and pass them in through the constructor.

steps.title: Why test doubles
steps.body:
Real units have **dependencies**: a database, an HTTP client, the clock, an email service. Using the real thing makes a test slow, flaky, or dangerous (nobody wants tests that email customers).

A **test double** is a stand-in you control:

- **Stub** — returns canned answers (`findUser(42)` → Ada). Feeds data *in*.
- **Mock** — records calls so the test can **verify** them. Checks what goes *out*.
- **Fake** — a working, lightweight implementation, like an in-memory repository instead of a database.
- **Spy** — wraps a real object: real methods run, calls get recorded.

steps.title: Dependency injection makes it possible

steps.prompt: You're testing `ReportService`, which reads sales figures from a `SalesRepository`. You just need the repository to hand back a fixed list. Which double fits best?
choices: A mock whose calls you verify
A spy wrapping the real database repository
A stub that returns a fixed list
No double — use the production database
steps.explanation: The repository is a *source of data* for the code under test, so a stub is enough: return the list, then assert on the report. Verifying the query call adds nothing — if the report is right, the data was clearly fetched.

steps.prompt: `SignupService.register(email)` should send a welcome email through `EmailSender.send(to, subject)`, and returns nothing useful. How do you test that behavior?
choices: Use a mock `EmailSender` and verify `send` was called with the new user's address
Assert on the return value of `register`
Send a real email and check the inbox in the test
Stub `send` to return `true` and assert nothing
steps.explanation: The behavior *is* an outgoing call with no visible return value — exactly what mocks are for. Verifying `send("ada@example.com", "Welcome!")` checks the effect without touching a real mail server.

steps.title: A hand-written fake
steps.problem: `UserService` depends on a `UserRepository` interface with `save(user)` and `findByEmail(email)`. Test that registering the same email twice is rejected — without a database.
steps: Write a fake: `InMemoryUserRepository` implements `UserRepository` with a `HashMap<String, User>` inside — `save` puts, `findByEmail` gets.
Arrange: `UserService service = new UserService(new InMemoryUserRepository());` then register `"ada@example.com"` once.
Act + Assert: `assertThrows(DuplicateEmailException.class, () -> service.register("ada@example.com"));`
steps.answer: The fake *remembers* what was saved, so the test exercises real behavior in milliseconds. Fakes shine when the code writes data and reads it back.

steps.prompt:
Why is this hard to unit test?

```python
class WeatherAlert:
    def check(self, city):
        data = requests.get(f"https://api.weather.example/{city}").json()
        return data["temp"] > 35
```
choices: It makes its HTTP call internally, so a test can't hand it a double without patching
Methods on classes can't be unit tested
steps.explanation: The dependency is hard-wired. Inject it instead — `WeatherAlert(weather_client)` with a `get_temp(city)` method — and the test can pass a stub returning 36 or 35 to check both sides of the boundary, instantly and offline.

steps.prompt: Which kind of test double is each one?

items.text: `findUser(42)` always returns a hard-coded Ada
Returns an exchange rate of 1.1, whatever currency you ask for
Afterwards, the test verifies `send("ada@example.com", "Welcome!")` was called once
Does nothing itself; the test checks that `charge(30)` was called
An `InMemoryUserRepository` that keeps saved users in a `HashMap`
A working in-memory queue standing in for the real message broker
Wraps a real `ArrayList`: `add` really adds, and every call is recorded
The real `PriceCalculator` runs, and the test also checks `round()` was called twice

steps.hint: Stub: canned answers in. Mock: calls out, verified. Fake: a lightweight version that really works. Spy: the real object, with its calls recorded.
steps.explanation: **Stubs** only feed canned data *in*: a fixed user, a fixed rate. **Mocks** exist so their calls can be *verified*; their own behavior doesn't matter. **Fakes** really work, just lightly: a `HashMap` instead of a database, an in-memory queue instead of a broker. **Spies** wrap a real object, so real methods run and calls are recorded too. Choose by what the test needs: data in → stub, an outgoing call to check → mock, write-then-read behavior → fake.

steps.prompt: `SalesRepository` talks to the production database, which tests can't reach. This test passes a stub instead, so it should pass without a database, but it crashes. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error:
FAILED test_total_sales_adds_up_months - ConnectionError: could not connect to sales-db:5432
1 failed
steps.hint: The constructor receives a `repo`. Does it use it?
steps.explanation: The constructor accepts `repo` but then ignores it and builds a real `SalesRepository`, so the stub never gets used. That's a hard-wired dependency in disguise. Storing the argument (`self.repo = repo`) is real constructor injection: production passes the real repository, the test passes the stub, and the total is 400. Passing the stub by keyword, passing the class, or giving `repo` a default all leave line 3 throwing the stub away.

lessons.title: Mockito and unittest.mock
lessons.takeaway: Stub with `when(...).thenReturn(...)` or `return_value`, verify with `verify` or `assert_called_once_with`, patch names where they're looked up — and mock only the boundaries.

steps.title: Mockito in three moves

steps.prompt: You forget the `when(rates.rate("USD", "EUR")).thenReturn(0.5)` line. `rate` returns a `double`. What does the mock return when the code calls it?
steps.explanation: Mockito mocks are "nice": unstubbed methods return `0`/`0.0`, `false`, `null` or an empty collection. So `toEuros` returns 0.0 and the test fails with `expected: <50.0> but was: <0.0>` — a zero you didn't expect is a strong hint of a missing stub.

steps.title: unittest.mock in Python
steps.body:
```python
from unittest.mock import Mock

def test_converts_and_logs():
    rates = Mock()
    rates.rate.return_value = 0.5
    log = Mock()

    service = PriceService(rates, log)
    eur = service.to_euros(100)

    assert eur == 50
    log.record.assert_called_once_with("converted 100 USD")
```

- `return_value` stubs a result; `side_effect = SomeError(...)` makes the call raise.
- `assert_called_once_with(...)` verifies a call.
- A plain `Mock` accepts *any* attribute, even misspelled ones. `Mock(spec=ExchangeRates)` or `create_autospec(ExchangeRates)` rejects methods the real class doesn't have.

steps.prompt: Your `rates` mock should simulate the exchange service being down. Fill in the blank: `rates.rate.______ = ConnectionError("down")`
steps.explanation: Setting `side_effect` to an exception instance (or class) makes every call raise it — perfect for testing error handling. It can also be a list of values to return on successive calls, or a function to compute the result.

steps.prompt: Using `PriceService` from above (`to_euros` multiplies the amount by `self.rates.rate("USD", "EUR")`), this test should pass. Instead it crashes. Click the line with the bug.
steps.code:
def test_converts_and_logs():
    rates = Mock()
    rates.return_value = 0.5
    log = Mock()

    service = PriceService(rates, log)
    eur = service.to_euros(100)

    assert eur == 50
    log.record.assert_called_once_with("converted 100 USD")
steps.error: TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for *: 'int' and 'Mock'
steps.hint: The code calls `rates.rate(...)`, not `rates(...)`.
steps.explanation: `rates.return_value` stubs what calling `rates(...)` itself returns. The code calls the **method** `rates.rate(...)`, which is a separate, unstubbed child mock that returns another `Mock`, and `100 * Mock` is a `TypeError`. Stub the method: `rates.rate.return_value = 0.5`. `rates.rate = 0.5` replaces the method with a float ("'float' object is not callable"), `Mock(return_value=0.5)` is the same mistake as line 3, and the last option stubs the mock that `rate(...)` *returns*, not `rate` itself.

steps.title: Patch where it's looked up
steps.body:
When code fetches a dependency itself, `unittest.mock.patch` swaps it temporarily — but you must patch the name **where it's used**, not where it's defined.

```python
# weather.py
from requests import get

def is_hot(city):
    return get(f"https://api.example/{city}").json()["temp"] > 35
```

```python
# test_weather.py
from unittest.mock import patch
from weather import is_hot

@patch("weather.get")
def test_is_hot(mock_get):
    mock_get.return_value.json.return_value = {"temp": 36}
    assert is_hot("Seville") is True
```

`from requests import get` copied the name into `weather`, so `weather.get` is what the code actually calls.

steps.prompt: `billing.py` does `from payments import charge_card` and calls `charge_card(...)` inside `checkout()`. Which patch stops your test of `billing.checkout()` from charging a real card?
steps.explanation: The `from ... import` created a second name, `billing.charge_card`, pointing at the real function. Patching `payments.charge_card` replaces only the original name — `checkout` still calls the real one. `patch` needs a full dotted path, so plain `"charge_card"` is an error, and `billing` has no `payments` attribute at all.
steps.hint: In which module's namespace does `checkout()` look the name up when it runs?

steps.title: Don't over-mock
steps.body:
- Mock **boundaries**: network, database, file system, clock, email, other services.
- Use **real objects** for plain values and simple in-process logic (`Money`, `Item`, lists).
- **Stub queries, verify commands.** Don't `verify` a call you only stubbed for its return value — asserting the result already proves it was used.
- If a test needs five mocks, the class under test probably does too much.

Over-mocked tests pass when the code is broken and fail when it's merely refactored — the worst of both worlds.

choices: Mockito can only mock interfaces, not classes
It never checks the total — only *how* it was computed — so a wrong sum still passes
The cart should be created in `@BeforeEach`
steps.explanation: If `total()` returned 12 instead of 7, this test would still pass. Use real items — `new Item(3)`, `new Item(4)` — and `assertEquals(7, cart.total())`. Items are simple values; there's nothing to gain from mocking them. (And Mockito mocks classes just fine.)
steps.hint: What happens to this test if `total()` returns the wrong number?

units.title: Testing well
units.description: TDD, flaky tests, coverage and the shape of a healthy test suite.

lessons.title: Test-driven development: red, green, refactor
lessons.takeaway: TDD loops in minutes: write a failing test (red), the simplest code that passes (green), then clean up while the tests keep you safe (refactor).

steps.title: The loop
steps.body:
**Test-driven development** flips the usual order: the test comes first.

- **Red** — write a small test for the next bit of behavior. Run it and *watch it fail*.
- **Green** — write the simplest code that makes it pass. Naive is fine.
- **Refactor** — clean up code and tests while everything stays green.

Each loop takes minutes. Every line of code is justified by a test, the design is shaped by how it's *used*, and you're never far from a working state.

steps.title: FizzBuzz, TDD-style
steps.problem: Build `fizzbuzz(n)` in Python, test first. It returns `"Fizz"` for multiples of 3, `"Buzz"` for multiples of 5, `"FizzBuzz"` for both, otherwise the number as text.
steps: Red: `assert fizzbuzz(1) == "1"` fails — the function doesn't exist yet. Green: `return str(n)`.
Red: `assert fizzbuzz(3) == "Fizz"`. Green: add `if n % 3 == 0: return "Fizz"`.
Red: `assert fizzbuzz(5) == "Buzz"`. Green: add the `n % 5` branch.
Red: `assert fizzbuzz(15) == "FizzBuzz"` fails — it returns `"Fizz"`, because the 3-check runs first. Green: check `n % 15` before the others.
Refactor: tidy the code; all four tests stay green.
steps.answer: Each rule arrived with a test that demanded it, and the 15 case exposed the ordering bug the moment it mattered.

steps.prompt: Why run the new test and watch it fail **before** writing the code?
choices: Test runners require at least one failure per run
To prove the test can actually detect the missing behavior — a test that passes straight away may be checking nothing
To measure how slow the test is
It's optional ceremony with no real purpose
steps.explanation: A test that has never failed has never proven it *can* fail. Typos in the assertion, a test that never runs, or checking the wrong thing all show up as an unexpected green at this step.

steps.prompt: You're in the Green step. The only test so far is `assert is_even(4) is True`. What's the TDD move?
choices: Write the simplest thing that passes, even if naive — the next tests (like `is_even(3)`) will force the general solution
Write the full, optimized solution covering every case you can think of
Write five more tests before writing any code
steps.explanation: Green is about getting to passing quickly. Code that's more general than the tests demand is untested code. Add a test like `is_even(3) is False` and the naive version is forced to become `n % 2 == 0`.

steps.title: Where TDD pays off most
steps.body:
TDD shines for logic with clear inputs and outputs: parsers, pricing rules, validation, algorithms. It's less natural for exploratory spikes or UI layout.

Even if you never do strict TDD, steal its best habit for **bug fixes**: first write a test that **reproduces the bug** and fails, then fix the code until it passes. You prove the fix works, and the bug can never quietly come back.

steps.prompt: During the Refactor step you rename variables and extract a helper, and a test goes red. What does that tell you?
choices: Refactoring always breaks tests, so ignore it
Delete the failing test — it was out of date
The refactor changed behavior (or the test depends on internals) — fix or undo it before moving on
steps.explanation: A refactor should change structure, not behavior, so the suite should stay green. Red means either you broke something — undo is cheap, since you changed only a little — or the test was coupled to implementation details and should be rewritten against the public API.

steps.prompt: You're adding the next feature TDD-style. Put one full loop in order.
items: Write a small test for the next bit of behavior
Run it and watch it fail
Write the simplest code that makes it pass
Run the tests and see them all pass
Clean up the code while every test stays green
steps.hint: Red, green, refactor, and the test always comes first.
steps.explanation: That's **red → green → refactor**. The test comes first and must fail, which proves it can detect the missing behavior. Then the simplest code that passes, confirmed by a green run. Only with everything green is it safe to refactor: any test that turns red now points straight at the change you just made. Then the loop starts again with the next test.

lessons.title: Flaky tests and determinism
lessons.takeaway: A test must give the same result every run: control time, randomness and shared state by injecting them, never by hoping.

steps.title: Where flakiness comes from
steps.body:
A **flaky test** passes sometimes and fails sometimes with no code change. Soon the team ignores red builds — and misses real bugs. Usual causes:

- **Time** — `LocalDate.now()`, `datetime.now()`, time zones, midnight
- **Randomness** — unseeded random numbers, generated IDs
- **Order & shared state** — static fields, a shared database row or file
- **Concurrency & real I/O** — `sleep` "until it's probably done", real network calls
- **Unordered collections** — asserting the iteration order of a `HashSet` or a Python `set`

choices: The code reads the real clock, which the test doesn't control
JUnit runs tests in random order
steps.explanation: The result depends on an input — the current time — that the test can't set. Make time an explicit input (next step) and the test becomes deterministic.

steps.title: Injecting the clock
steps.problem: Make `Greeter.greet()` testable at any hour of the day.
steps: Java has a ready-made seam, `java.time.Clock`. Pass one in — `new Greeter(clock)` — and call `LocalTime.now(clock)` inside.
Production code passes `Clock.systemDefaultZone()`.
The test passes a frozen clock: `Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2024-01-01T09:00:00Z"), ZoneOffset.UTC)`, then asserts `"Good morning"`.
In Python, do the same by injecting a `now` function — `Greeter(now=lambda: datetime(2024, 1, 1, 9, 0))` — or patch it.
steps.answer: Time becomes an input you control: the test passes at 3 p.m., at midnight and on New Year's Eve — and you can test the afternoon greeting too.

steps.prompt: `shuffle_deck()` uses Python's `random.shuffle`. A test asserts the first card is the Ace of Spades, and passes about 2% of the time. Best fix?
choices: Run the test 50 times and pass if any run passes
Inject a seeded `random.Random(42)`, or assert properties that always hold, like "52 unique cards"
steps.explanation: Randomness, like time, should be an input. A seeded generator makes the shuffle reproducible; property checks (same 52 cards, no duplicates) don't depend on the order at all. 2% ≈ 1 in 52 — the test was just getting lucky.

steps.prompt: This test passes on some runs and fails on others, with no code change. Click the line that makes it flaky.
steps.error:
Run 1: 1 passed
Run 2: 1 failed
E       AssertionError: assert ['python', 'ci', 'testing'] == ['python', 'testing', 'ci']
fixes: Change line 2 to `return [tag for post in posts for tag in post['tags']]`
Add `random.seed(0)` before line 5 (and `import random` at the top)
steps.hint: In what order does a `set` of strings hand back its items?
steps.explanation: `unique_tags` builds a **set**, and a set has no defined order: Python randomizes string hashes in every new process, so the list comes out in a different order from run to run. The test asserts one particular order. Sorting both sides checks *which* tags came back, which is the real contract. Comparing with a different fixed order is just as flaky, a list comprehension keeps the duplicate `'testing'` and fails every time, and `random.seed` doesn't touch hash randomization.

steps.title: Don't sleep — wait or remove the wait
steps.body:
`Thread.sleep(500)` or `time.sleep(0.5)` "to let the background job finish" is a classic flake: too short on a busy CI machine, wasted time everywhere else.

Better options:

- In unit tests, make the work **synchronous** — inject an executor that runs tasks immediately.
- When you truly must wait, **poll for the condition** with a timeout (e.g. Awaitility in Java).

And never "fix" flakiness with automatic retries alone: that hides a real bug, sometimes one your users will hit.

steps.prompt: Test A adds a user to a shared static list; Test B asserts the list is empty. B passes when it runs first and fails when A runs first. What's going on?
choices: Order dependence through shared state — give each test fresh state in `@BeforeEach` or a fixture
steps.explanation: Each test must set up everything it relies on and leave nothing behind. Fresh state per test makes order irrelevant — which also lets you run tests in parallel.

steps.prompt: Sort each test ingredient: can it make a test flaky, or does it give the same result on every run?
buckets: Can flake: depends on something the test doesn't control

items.text: Asserting `greet()`'s result when it reads `datetime.now()` internally
Shuffling with an unseeded `random.shuffle`
`time.sleep(0.5)` to let a background job finish
Asserting `list(tags)` equals a fixed list, where `tags` is a set of strings
Two tests that add to and read the same static list
A unit test that calls a real third-party weather API
Passing the greeter a `Clock.fixed(...)` set to 9 a.m.
Shuffling with an injected `random.Random(42)`
Comparing `sorted(result)` with an expected list
Each test creating its own fresh list in `@BeforeEach`

steps.hint: Ask: could this give a different result tomorrow, on another machine, or in another test order?
steps.explanation: Flaky tests depend on an input the test doesn't set: the real clock, unseeded randomness, timing (`sleep`), hash order, shared state left by another test, or a real network. Each deterministic version turns that input into something the test controls: a fixed clock, a seeded generator, an order-independent comparison, fresh state per test.

lessons.title: Coverage and the test pyramid
lessons.takeaway: Coverage shows what your tests never ran, not whether they check anything; build many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and a handful of end-to-end tests.

steps.title: Line vs branch coverage
steps.body:
**Coverage** measures which code ran while your tests ran.

- **Line coverage** — the % of lines executed
- **Branch coverage** — the % of decision outcomes taken: every `if` both true *and* false

Tools: **JaCoCo** for Java and Kotlin; **coverage.py** for Python, usually through **pytest-cov** (`pytest --cov`).

steps.title: 100% of lines, half the branches
steps.problem:
```python
def shipping(total):
    fee = 5
    if total >= 50:
        fee = 0
    return fee
```

The only test is `assert shipping(80) == 0`.
steps: With a total of 80, every line runs: `fee = 5`, the `if`, `fee = 0`, `return`. Line coverage: **100%**.
But the `if` was only ever true. The path where the condition is false — the fee stays 5 — never ran. Branch coverage: **50%**.
Add `assert shipping(20) == 5`, plus the boundary `assert shipping(50) == 0`.
steps.answer: Line coverage can hit 100% while whole paths go untested. Branch coverage is the more honest number.

steps.prompt: A test calls `calculate_tax(100)` but contains **no assertion**. What happens to coverage?
choices: Coverage stays the same, because nothing is asserted
The coverage tool reports an error
Coverage goes up, even though the test can't catch a wrong result
steps.explanation: Coverage counts *execution*, not *checking*. An assertion-free test executes code and inflates the number while catching nothing except crashes.

steps.title: Why 100% isn't the goal
steps.body:
Coverage is great at one thing: revealing code that **no test ever ran**. Those gaps deserve a look.

It's a poor *target*. Chasing 100% breeds tests of trivial getters and assertion-free tests that pump up the number. Many teams aim for roughly 70–90% and concentrate on risky logic.

The better question is: *if I broke this line, would a test fail?* **Mutation testing** tools (PIT for Java, mutmut for Python) check exactly that, automatically.

steps.title: The test pyramid
steps.body:
- **Many unit tests** at the base — milliseconds each, pinpoint failures
- **Fewer integration tests** in the middle — a real database, real HTTP between your components; slower, but they catch wiring mistakes
- **A few end-to-end tests** at the top — drive the whole app like a user; slowest and most brittle

Turn it upside down — mostly slow end-to-end tests, the "ice-cream cone" — and you get slow feedback and failures that are hard to diagnose.

steps.prompt: Your unit tests pass using a mocked repository, but in production the SQL query has a typo in a column name. Which test would have caught it?
choices: Another unit test with a mocked repository
An integration test that runs the query against a real database (e.g. one started in a container)
steps.explanation: A mock never executes SQL, so no unit test can see the typo. That's exactly the gap integration tests fill: the seams between your code and real infrastructure.

steps.prompt: A suite has 20 unit tests and 400 browser-driven end-to-end tests. It takes 2 hours and fails randomly. What's the best direction?
choices: Add more end-to-end tests to cover the failures
Run the end-to-end tests less often and delete the unit tests
Push most checks down into unit and integration tests; keep a few end-to-end tests for critical user journeys
steps.explanation: Most rules (validation, pricing, edge cases) can be checked by unit tests in milliseconds. Keep end-to-end tests for "can a user sign up and check out?" — the few journeys where the whole system must work together.

steps.prompt: Which layer of the test pyramid does each test belong to?

items.text: `shipping(20) == 5`, checked in memory in a millisecond
Password rules checked with the user repository mocked out
A parameterized test of a date-parsing function
A repository's SQL query run against a real Postgres started in a container
Saving an order through the repository, then reading it back from a real database
Checking your consumer really reads messages from a Kafka broker in a container
A browser script signs up, fills a cart and checks out on the running app
Logging in through the real UI and checking the dashboard loads

steps.hint: Unit: your code alone, with fakes or mocks. Integration: your code plus one real piece of infrastructure. End-to-end: the whole app, driven like a user.
steps.explanation: **Unit** tests run your logic alone, in milliseconds, with collaborators mocked or faked. **Integration** tests check a seam between your code and something real, such as a database or a message broker, so they catch wiring mistakes like a typo in SQL. **End-to-end** tests drive the whole system through its UI like a user: valuable for a few critical journeys, but the slowest and most brittle, which is why they sit at the narrow top.
